transcript.content: Hello. What brings you in to see me today?
I'm here because I constantly feel like I'm on the go and just can't seem to slow down. It honestly feels like I'm being driven by a motor all the time, and I don't know how to turn it off.
Have you felt this way for as long as you can remember, even back in childhood, or does this feeling come and go in distinct periods or episodes?

It definitely doesn't come and go in episodes; I've felt this way constantly since I was a kid, well before I was 12. It has been a really consistent, everyday struggle for at least a year and three months now.
In addition to feeling constantly on the go, do you also struggle with paying attention, staying organized, or being easily distracted?

No, I don't really struggle with paying attention or staying organized. I'm actually pretty good at keeping track of my things and focusing when I need to. It's really just the constant physical restlessness and always needing to be on the move that is the issue for me.

latest_inference.note: Previously, the candidates were Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation), Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Hyperactive/Impulsive Presentation), and Generalized Anxiety Disorder. Based on the patient's explicit denial of difficulties with attention, organization, or focus, the Combined Presentation of ADHD is ruled out. Furthermore, the patient describes a lifelong, constant physical restlessness ('driven by a motor') starting well before age 12 without prominent excessive worry or anxiety, ruling out Generalized Anxiety Disorder. Therefore, the diagnosis is narrowed down to Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Hyperactive/Impulsive Presentation).

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports a persistent, lifelong pattern of hyperactivity and physical restlessness, describing a feeling of being 'driven by a motor' since childhood (prior to age 12). The absence of attention or organizational difficulties rules out the Combined Presentation, and the continuous, non-episodic course rules out mood disorders such as Bipolar I Disorder.
